[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report longitudinal data (2000-2020) merged with national ecological footprint accounts from the Global Footprint Network — This allows direct testing of the hypothesis by comparing correlations between GDP growth and subjective well-being across country-year panels stratified by ecological debt levels.

[PATH:empirical] Panel regression analysis of OECD and developing countries using the Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) as an alternative to GDP growth, paired with Gallup World Poll well-being measures — GPI accounts for environmental degradation and resource depletion, making it possible to assess whether the hypothesized moderation effect is robust to alternative measures of economic performance.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical literature on the 'Easterlin Paradox' and the 'Threshold Hypothesis' in ecological economics (e.g., work by Easterlin, Kahneman, and Daly) — This literature suggests that beyond a certain point, further GDP growth yields diminishing returns to well-being, especially when ecological costs are high, providing a theoretical framework to interpret the hypothesized pattern.

scope.domain: low vs. high ecological debt countries

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey and World Bank (2000-2020) comparing subjective well-being trends with GDP growth rates in countries with low ecological debt (e.g., using the Ecological Footprint Network's national debt classifications). — Directly tests the hypothesized negative relationship by analyzing well-being changes alongside economic growth in the specified country group over the stated time period.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of low ecological debt countries (e.g., Costa Rica, Bhutan) that have experienced rapid GDP growth, examining qualitative and quantitative evidence of well-being shifts (e.g., through Gallup surveys or national happiness indices). — Provides context-specific depth to identify whether growth correlates with well-being declines, controlling for cultural or policy factors that might confound aggregate data.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of theoretical literature on the Easterlin Paradox and the 'threshold hypothesis' in environmental economics, focusing on studies that model well-being as a function of growth under ecological constraints. — Establishes whether existing theoretical frameworks predict or explain a negative effect in low-debt contexts, helping to interpret empirical findings and refine the hypothesis.

C007.subject: GDP growth
C007.object: national subjective well-being in countries with high ecological debt, when mediated by perceived environmental degradation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: GDP growth national subjective well-being in countries with high ecological debt, when mediated by perceived environmental degradation]

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal panel data from the World Values Survey and Ecological Footprint Network, focusing on high ecological debt countries (e.g., Brazil, India) over 5-10 years, measuring GDP growth, perceived environmental degradation (e.g., self-reported air/water quality), and life satisfaction. — Directly tests the mediated pathway: GDP growth → perceived environmental degradation → subjective well-being. Panel data can establish temporal precedence and control for confounds.

[PATH:empirical] Experimental or quasi-experimental studies using vignettes or natural experiments (e.g., sudden industrial booms or recessions in high ecological debt regions) to manipulate perceived environmental degradation and measure well-being. — Provides causal evidence for the mediation mechanism by isolating the effect of perceived degradation on well-being independent of other GDP-related changes.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical review of the 'Easterlin Paradox' and 'environmental Kuznets curve' literature, specifically examining cases where economic growth in ecologically stressed nations fails to improve or reduces happiness. — Synthesizes existing findings on the conditional relationship between growth and well-being, identifying gaps in mediation by environmental perceptions and informing model specification.

[PATH:empirical] World Happiness Report panel data (2000-2020) merged with World Bank ecological footprint and GDP per capita data for high ecological debt countries — Directly tests the hypothesis by correlating GDP growth with subjective well-being measures (e.g., Cantril ladder) in countries with ecological debt above a threshold, controlling for confounds like inequality and governance.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of high ecological debt countries (e.g., Costa Rica vs. resource-extractive economies) using qualitative interviews and longitudinal well-being surveys — Provides context-specific mechanisms (e.g., trade-offs between material gains and environmental degradation) that can confirm or refute the causal direction and boundary conditions of the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models from ecological economics (e.g., Daly's steady-state economy theory, Easterlin paradox critiques) applied to high-debt contexts — Offers a conceptual framework to predict when GDP growth might fail to enhance well-being due to ecological constraints, informing empirical design and interpretation of results.
